say.text: Worked case first. A 28-year-old woman has **right iliac fossa (RIF)** pain for 14 hours and irregular periods.

**Step 1** is a **beta-hCG** (human chorionic gonadotropin) test, before any scan. An ectopic pregnancy changes both the imaging and the surgery, so pregnancy is excluded first in every woman of reproductive age.
**Step 2**: the beta-hCG is negative and she is an adult, so **contrast-enhanced CT (CECT)** is the most accurate test here.
A classmate planned this for a 26-year-old woman with RIF pain and irregular periods.
'Step 1: contrast CT abdomen to settle the diagnosis. Step 2: beta-hCG only if the scan is normal.'
Which is the error in this plan?

choices.label: The pregnancy test should come before imaging
Nothing is wrong; settling the appendix comes first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the first result could change. Could this pain be something other than the appendix, and would that change what you do next?
That is the working-diagnosis model: the appendix is the likely cause, so scanning it feels like the first job.
Look at the patient before the scan. What could she have that would change the next step?

sure_note.text: You were sure. Re-check the first step: what has to be settled before any imaging in this woman?

say.text: That is the surgeon's model: a RIF pain that is not settling goes to theatre to be looked at.
Before any operation, which test would change the plan in this woman?

sure_note.text: You were sure. The operation is the last step here, not the first.

say.text: Try once more. The same classmate plan:
'Step 1: contrast CT abdomen to settle the diagnosis. Step 2: beta-hCG only if the scan is normal.'
Which is the error?

choices.label: Nothing is wrong; settling the appendix comes first
The pregnancy test should come before imaging

say.text: Tempting: the appendix is the working diagnosis, and contrast CT is the most accurate test in an adult.
Why it is wrong: in any woman of reproductive age, beta-hCG comes first, because an ectopic pregnancy changes both the imaging and the surgery.
Right: beta-hCG first, then imaging for the appendix.
Tempting: a RIF pain that is not settling makes a surgeon want to look, so the operation feels like the decisive step.
Why it is wrong: an ectopic pregnancy changes the operation itself, so the pregnancy test has to come before theatre.
Right: beta-hCG first; for a non-pregnant adult, contrast CT is the most accurate test before the knife.
Yes. The pregnancy test comes before any imaging in a woman of reproductive age, because an ectopic pregnancy changes the next step.
A classmate's answer for a 20-week pregnant woman with RIF pain was:
'MRI first, because it is the most accurate test.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Keep MRI first, as it is the most accurate
Ultrasound first, then MRI if it is unclear
Contrast CT first, as it is the most accurate
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the first test is for in this patient group. Accuracy is only one criterion when you choose the first test.
That is the accuracy model: rank the tests by how good they are, and MRI comes out on top.
The first test is a rung on a ladder, not the best test on paper. Which rung is this patient on?

sure_note.text: You were sure that accuracy sets the order. Check the ladder again before you choose.

say.text: That is the adult model: contrast CT is the most accurate test, so it seems to go first for everyone.
Who is the patient? Ask that before you ask which test is most accurate.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check the patient group first, then the test.

say.text: Try again. The same classmate's answer:
'MRI first, because it is the most accurate test.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Contrast CT first, as it is the most accurate
Keep MRI first, as it is the most accurate
Ultrasound first, then MRI if it is unclear

say.text: Tempting: MRI is accurate, and the most accurate test feels like the right first test.
Why it is wrong: in pregnancy, ultrasound is the first test, and MRI without gadolinium is the second rung, used when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Right: ultrasound first, then MRI if it is unclear, then surgery as indicated.
Tempting: contrast CT is the most accurate test, and in adults it is the test of choice, so it feels right for any patient.
Why it is wrong: the patient group changes the first test. In pregnancy, the first test is ultrasound.
Right: ultrasound first, then MRI if it is unclear.
Yes. In pregnancy, ultrasound is the first rung. MRI without gadolinium comes next if ultrasound is inconclusive.
The same test, three patients. In which one is contrast CT the test of choice?

choices.label: A pregnant woman at 26 weeks with RIF pain

say.text: Tempting: the child has the same pain, and CT is the most accurate test, so it looks like the answer at any age.
Why it is wrong: in a child, the first test is ultrasound, because age sets the first rung.
Right: contrast CT belongs to the adult with equivocal signs.
Tempting: a pregnant woman with pain also needs a scan, and CT is the most accurate test, so it looks like the first choice.
Why it is wrong: pregnancy changes the first test. Ultrasound comes first, then MRI if it is unclear.
Right: contrast CT is the adult's test of choice, not the first test in pregnancy.
Yes. Contrast CT is the test of choice in an adult; in a child or a pregnant woman, ultrasound is first.
Which statement about ultrasound in suspected appendicitis in an adult is correct?

choices.label: A normal ultrasound rules appendicitis out in adults
A negative scan does not exclude it; CT is better
Ultrasound is the most accurate test in adults

say.text: Tempting: a clean scan feels final, and ultrasound was the first test, so the work-up seems finished.
Why it is wrong: in an adult, a scan that shows nothing does not exclude appendicitis; the next test is contrast CT.
Right: ultrasound starts the work-up, and a negative or unclear result in an adult moves on to CT.
Tempting: ultrasound was the investigation of choice in older exam keys, so it still feels like the most accurate test.
Why it is wrong: current practice keeps ultrasound first in children and pregnancy, but in adults contrast CT is the most accurate test.
Right: read the patient before naming the test; in an adult, contrast CT is the answer for accuracy.
Yes. A negative or unclear ultrasound does not close the case in an adult; contrast CT is the more accurate test.
A woman of reproductive age has suspected appendicitis and may be pregnant. Which pathway is right?

choices.label: Beta-hCG, MRI first, ultrasound if unclear, surgery
Ultrasound, then surgery, beta-hCG only if normal
Beta-hCG, ultrasound, MRI if unclear, then surgery

say.text: Tempting: MRI is the most accurate test in pregnancy, so it seems to belong first in the pathway.
Why it is wrong: ultrasound is the first rung in pregnancy, and MRI without gadolinium is the second rung, used when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Right: beta-hCG, then ultrasound, then MRI if unclear, then surgery as indicated.
Tempting: the imaging is the working step, and the pregnancy test feels like a formality to do later.
Why it is wrong: beta-hCG comes before imaging in every woman of reproductive age, because an ectopic pregnancy changes the next step.
Right: beta-hCG first, then the imaging ladder, then surgery as indicated.
Yes. Beta-hCG comes first, then the ladder: ultrasound first, and MRI second if ultrasound is unclear.
A 45-year-old man has persisting RIF tenderness and a rising count. Ultrasound could not show the appendix. What is the next step?

choices.label: Repeat ultrasound, as it is the investigation of choice
Discharge, as ultrasound has excluded appendicitis
Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen, the next test in adults

say.text: Tempting: the scan was done and found nothing, so the work-up feels finished and discharge looks safe.
Why it is wrong: an ultrasound that does not show the appendix does not exclude appendicitis in an adult.
Right: with persisting tenderness and a rising count, the next step is contrast CT, the most accurate test in adults.
Tempting: ultrasound was the investigation of choice in older exam keys, so repeating it feels like the textbook answer.
Why it is wrong: current practice uses ultrasound first in children and pregnancy; in an adult it has already been done, and CT is more accurate.
Right: contrast CT abdomen, the most accurate test for an adult.
Yes. An unhelpful ultrasound does not end the work-up in an adult; contrast CT is the next test.
The Alvarado (MANTRELS) score totals 10. Which two items score 2 points each?

choices.label: Migration of pain and rebound tenderness
Tenderness in RIF and rebound tenderness

say.text: Tempting: migration and rebound are classic signs, so they feel like the heavy items in the score.
Why it is wrong: only tenderness in the RIF and leucocytosis score 2; every other item, migration and rebound included, scores 1.
Right: RIF tenderness and leucocytosis carry the 2s, and the whole score totals 10.
Tempting: rebound is the sign taught as the most specific, so it feels like a 2-point item.
Why it is wrong: rebound tenderness scores 1; only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2.
Right: the 2-point items are RIF tenderness and leucocytosis, and the total is 10.
Yes. RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2 each; the other items score 1 each.
A man with migration of pain, nausea, RIF tenderness, rebound tenderness and leucocytosis. What is his Alvarado total?
Tempting: migration and rebound feel like specific signs, so you score each one as 2.
Why it is wrong: migration and rebound each score 1. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2.
Right: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7. A score of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely, not certain.
Tempting: leucocytosis feels like an ordinary blood result, so it gets scored as 1 like the rest.
Why it is wrong: leucocytosis scores 2, not 1, and it is one of the two items that do.
Right: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7, and a score of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely.
Yes. The total is 7: migration 1, nausea 1, RIF tenderness 2, rebound 1, leucocytosis 2.
